issues.display_title: Issue #57: Collab: project members & authz API (sub-project 1/3)
issues.main_description_html:
Collaboration — Sub-project 1/3: Project Members & Authz API

Assigned to: Ibnu Rizqia Ramadan — Developer

Foundation for real-time collaborative floorplan editing: persistent membership + role, and the authz endpoint the socket server & FE gate consume.

Scope

  • ProjectMember model (viewer/editor) + AutoMigrate; owner implicit via Project.UserID.
  • Pure decideRole + FetchRole(userID, projectID) authz helper.
  • Endpoints under /projects/:id:
    • GET /access → effective role owner|editor|viewer|none
    • GET /members, POST /members (invite by email), PATCH /members/:userId, DELETE /members/:userId
  • Trust boundary: every mutation re-resolves role server-side. Owner-only member management.

Docs

  • Spec: docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-03-project-members-collab-authz-design.md
  • Plan: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-03-project-members-collab-authz.md (7 tasks, TDD)

Definition of Done

  • Build + vet + go test ./src/action/v1/members/ green
  • /access contract stable for socket + FE sub-projects

RESULT

Implemented on branch feature/57-project-members-authz (7 commits, TDD, per-task reviewed).

Added (src/action/v1/members/, src/controllers/v1/members/, src/models/models.go, src/routes/v1/projects.go):

  • ProjectMember model (viewer/editor, no soft-delete, OTP-pattern UUID) + AutoMigrate.
  • Pure decideRole (unit-tested, total) + FetchRole authz core. Owner implicit via Project.UserID.
  • Endpoints under /projects/:id: GET /access (owner|editor|viewer|none, never 403), GET /members, POST /members (invite by email, upsert), PATCH /members/:userId, DELETE /members/:userId. Owner-only for member management; server-side role re-resolution on every write (trust boundary).

Verification: go build ./..., go vet ./..., go test ./src/action/v1/members/..., gofmt -l all clean. Live curl smoke (needs dev DB + tokens) pending — commands in plan Task 7.

Final review (opus): READY TO MERGE, 0 critical/important. Optional follow-up: consolidate FetchRole to return the project owner so list.go/create.go drop a redundant re-fetch.

issues.display_title: Issue #52: Thumbnail from first floor_configs level image
issues.main_description_html:
Thumbnail from first floor_configs level image

Change

thumbnail_url now derives from the first level in floor_configs that has a fileName (the image actually shown in the editor), instead of the earliest project_files upload — which was frequently an orphaned/replaced file. Also removes the per-project N+1 query.

Acceptance

  • Dashboard thumbnail matches the first level's floormap image.
  • Levels without an image fall through to the next; none -> "" (frontend default).
  • No extra DB query per project.

RESULT

src/action/v1/project/shared.go: firstThumbnailURL parses floor_configs, returns first level with a fileName as /v1/projects/:id/file?name=. N+1 removed. go build + vet pass.

Commit: a64f8ad

Hard-delete project file records

Problem

DeleteProjectFile removed the file from disk but soft-deleted the project_files row (gorm DeletedAt). Rows accumulated indefinitely even though the underlying files were gone.

Fix

Use config.DB.Unscoped().Delete(&projectFile) to remove the row outright. Safe because the disk file is already removed just above.

Acceptance

  • Deleting a project file removes the disk file AND the DB row (no lingering soft-deleted rows).
  • project_files no longer grows on repeated image replace / level delete.

RESULT

src/action/v1/files/project_delete.go now uses config.DB.Unscoped().Delete(&projectFile). Disk file removed then row hard-deleted. go build + go vet pass.

Commit: 3392947

issues.main_description_html:
RESULT 18/06/26

✅ Implementation Complete — Ready for Unit Testing

Implementation :

e355def

Description

This task covers the initial setup of the gothru-maps-backend-go project. The goal is to establish a robust, modular, and scalable architecture using Go Fiber and GORM, following the architectural patterns of the reference repository.

Architecture Overview

  • Actions: Contain business logic and interact with the framework context (fiber.Ctx).
  • Controllers: Serve as thin entry points that delegate requests to Actions.
  • Routes: Organized by version (v1) and module, orchestrated by a central route manager.
  • Config: Centralized initialization for databases (MySQL/Postgres), Redis, and RabbitMQ.

Tech Stack

  • Language: Go 1.25.5
  • Web Framework: Fiber v2
  • ORM: GORM
  • Database Drivers: MySQL, PostgreSQL
  • Middleware: Logger, Recover
  • Services: Redis, RabbitMQ (AMQP)

Implementation Checklist

1. Environment & Dependencies

  • Initialize go.mod with core dependencies (Fiber, GORM, UUID, AMQP, Redis).
  • Create .env template for local configuration (Port, Database credentials).

2. Project Structure

  • Create standardized directory tree (cmd/api, cmd/workers, src/action/v1, src/controllers/v1, src/routes/v1, src/config, src/models, src/lib).

3. Core Implementation (Placeholder/Dev Module)

  • Implement Ping Action to handle health checks.
  • Implement Ping Controller as the API bridge.
  • Configure Route versioning (/api/v1) and register the dev module.
  • Set up Main Route Orchestrator to manage all module routes.

4. Main Application Entry Point

  • Implement cmd/api/main.go (config init, middleware, server startup, graceful exit, dynamic port binding).

Verification Result

  • Build Status: Success (Tested via go build).
  • Endpoints: GET /api/v1/ping verified.
  • Dependency Check: All requested libraries resolved in go.mod.

Task 2: Safe Error Messages for Users

Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-backend-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-backend-plan.md

Context

When something goes wrong inside the backend — a database error, a constraint violation, an unexpected failure — the system needs to tell the user something went wrong without revealing the technical details of how the system works internally. Raw database error messages often contain table names, column names, or query fragments that expose system internals and can be a security risk.

Goal

Create a single utility that intercepts any internal error and converts it into a clean, user-safe message before it is sent back to the caller.

What We're Building

A small helper function that takes any error the backend encounters and returns a safe string:

  • For database-specific errors: returns the human-readable message the database provides (e.g. "duplicate key value violates unique constraint") without any SQL or query text
  • For all other errors: returns just the first line of the message, stripping any technical stack trace

Why It Matters

Security and professionalism. Showing a user a raw SQL error like ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_email_key" on table "users" (INSERT INTO users ...) is both a poor experience and a potential security leak. This helper ensures every error response is clean, consistent, and safe.

Acceptance Criteria

  • A plain error message ("connection refused") passes through unchanged
  • A multi-line error message is trimmed to just the first line
  • A database constraint error returns the human-readable description without any SQL text
  • No raw SQL, table names, or query fragments appear in any error response

What Changes After This Task

All HTTP handlers can now safely return error details to callers without worrying about exposing internal system information. This helper is used by every handler from Task 6 onwards.

issues.display_title: Issue #4: Task 3: Session Tokens and Password Security
issues.main_description_html:
Task 3: Session Tokens and Password Security

Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-backend-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-backend-plan.md

Context

Two fundamental security operations underpin user accounts: proving who a user is (session tokens) and protecting their password (hashing). These are not UI features — they are the security primitives the rest of the auth system is built on top of. They need to be correct, tested, and isolated before any login or register logic is written.

Goal

Build the three cryptographic helpers the auth system depends on: generating and verifying session tokens, generating and verifying one-time link tokens (for email verification and password reset), and securely hashing and checking passwords.

What We're Building

  • Session token (JWT): A signed, time-limited credential issued after login. Carried in every subsequent request to prove the user is signed in. Expires after 30 days.
  • One-time link token: A random secret used in email verification and password reset links. Stored only as a hash — the raw value goes in the email link and is never stored.
  • Password hashing: Passwords are never stored in plain text. They are irreversibly hashed before storage and compared safely at login time.

Why It Matters

These are the lowest-level building blocks of the auth system. If session tokens can be forged or passwords can be reversed, the entire platform is compromised. Getting this layer right — and testing it thoroughly — protects everything built on top of it.

Acceptance Criteria

  • A session token is issued and can be verified to recover the original user ID and email
  • A session token has exactly three parts separated by dots (the standard JWT format)
  • Two separately generated one-time tokens are never identical
  • The raw one-time token and its stored hash are always different
  • A correct password passes the check; an incorrect password is rejected
  • No password is ever stored in readable form

What Changes After This Task

The login, register, email verification, and password reset handlers can now be built. These helpers are the security foundation they all depend on.

  • Session Token Standard (JWT HS256):
    • GenerateSessionToken(uniqueID) issues signed HS256 tokens carrying sub, exp, and iat.
    • Exactly 3 dot-separated parts verified (header.payload.signature).

    • CheckPassword correctly matches valid passwords and rejects mismatched/empty/whitespace passwords.
    • Distinct salts verified: Hashing the same password multiple times produces distinct ciphertext.

Summary

A single reusable authentication middleware that sits in front of protected routes: it verifies the session token, attaches the user's identity to the request, and rejects unauthenticated requests with 401 before any handler runs.

Deliverables

File Purpose

Behavior

Gate — Auth() fiber.Handler

  • Reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header.
  • Missing header / wrong scheme → 401, request stops.
  • Invalid or expired token → 401, request stops.
  • Valid token → decodes identity via utils.VerifySessionToken, stores userID + userEmail in c.Locals, calls c.Next().
  • 401 responses return a consistent JSON body { "success": false, "message": "unauthorized" } — no token internals leaked.

Companion helpers (called inside protected handlers)

  • UserID(c *fiber.Ctx) string — authenticated user's ID (or "").
  • UserEmail(c *fiber.Ctx) string — authenticated user's email (or "").

Usage

// inside handler:
uid := middleware.UserID(c)

Acceptance Criteria

  • Request with no Authorization header → 401
  • Request with a valid token → 200 and handler can read the user's ID
  • Request with an invalid or expired token → 401
  • User ID recovered inside the handler matches the one used to create the token (test: user-777)

Task 5: Request Authentication Gate

Docs

2026-06-19-floormap-backend-overview.md
2026-06-19-floormap-backend-plan.md

Context

Most of the backend's endpoints — projects, files, billing — should only be accessible to signed-in users. Rather than writing "is this user signed in?" checks inside every handler, this task creates a single reusable gate that sits in front of protected routes and automatically blocks unauthenticated requests.

Goal

Build the authentication middleware: a piece of logic that intercepts every request to a protected route, checks for a valid session token, and either lets the request through (attaching the user's identity) or rejects it with a 401 Unauthorized response.

What We're Building

  • A gate function that reads the Authorization: Bearer <token> header from every incoming request
  • If the token is missing or invalid: returns 401 immediately, request goes no further
  • If the token is valid: decodes the user's identity from it and makes that identity available to the handler downstream
  • A companion helper that handlers call to retrieve the signed-in user's details from the request

Why It Matters

Without this gate, any handler that doesn't implement its own auth check could be called by anyone. This middleware makes the protected/unprotected boundary explicit and enforced in one place. All project, file, and billing handlers depend on it.

Acceptance Criteria

  • A request with no Authorization header receives a 401 response
  • A request with a valid token receives a 200 response and the handler can read the user's ID
  • A request with an invalid or expired token receives a 401 response
  • The user's ID recovered inside the handler matches the one used to create the token

What Changes After This Task

Protected routes (projects, files, billing) can now be wrapped with this gate and trust that any request that reaches them has a verified, identified user behind it.

1. Technical Evaluation & Code Architecture Verification

  • Middleware Interception Architecture (Auth()):
    • Scans Authorization: Bearer <token> header. Missing header, wrong scheme (Basic ...), or empty bearer token terminates the request before downstream handlers run.
    • Validates session tokens through utils.VerifySessionToken(token).
    • Database-backed identity binding: Looks up users table with unique_id = userID. If the user does not exist or was deleted, request is rejected with 401 Unauthorized.
    • Context attachment: Stores authenticated *models.User in c.Locals("user"), retrievable via middleware.GetUser(c).
  • Role & Support Gate (SupportOnly()):
    • Verifies that user.Role == "support", returning 403 Forbidden for standard users or empty roles.
  • Graceful Anonymous Handling (OptionalUser()):
    • Valid token returns user, while missing/invalid token degrades safely to ok=false without aborting the context.
